name: OMAD / 36-hour fasts

lead: OMAD (one meal a day) packs all eating into a window of an hour or two, and 36-hour fasts leave a day and a half between meals. People use them to drop body fat quickly and get a leaner face with less bloat.

The pattern works mainly by lowering total calorie intake, and the fat loss that results shows in the face as it shows elsewhere. Most human studies of intermittent fasting report weight loss of roughly 2.5 to 9.9 percent, and some reviews show results similar to ordinary calorie restriction. Health bodies including the American Heart Association and the US National Institute on Aging describe the evidence as limited or inconclusive. Weight lost includes some lean mass.

paras: People pick a daily eating window or fast on set days, drinking water, black coffee or tea in between and eating one large meal, often high in protein. It is commonly paired with lifting to hold on to muscle. Results show as steady scale and mirror changes over weeks, depending on the calorie deficit.

Reported effects include hunger, dizziness, headaches and irritability. Fasting is not recommended for pregnancy, children, older adults or people prone to eating disorders, and prolonged fasts raise gallstone risk. Some lean mass is lost along with fat.

angle.text: Users eat one meal a day or fast for 36 hours to build a calorie deficit, lose body fat quickly and reveal a leaner face. Intermittent fasting trials show weight loss, with facial leanness following from overall fat loss rather than being measured directly.

lead: OMAD (one meal a day) is a form of time-restricted eating in which all daily food is eaten in a window of one to two hours; 36-hour fasts stretch the gap between meals beyond a day.[1] People use both in looksmaxxing communities to lose body fat quickly. Less body fat shows up as a leaner jawline and face, a more defined physique and, as some users put it, less morning bloat, which is why fasting features among the fat-loss tools discussed on looksmax.org.[2][3]

The practice is simple to describe: one large meal, with only water or non-caloric drinks the rest of the day, sometimes combined with low-carbohydrate eating, resistance training or weight-loss medication before a muscle-building phase.[1][2] Lifters on T Nation likewise describe adopting OMAD as part of cuts or as a fit with a busy life.[4][5][6]

Intermittent fasting as a category has been studied far more than OMAD itself. Reviews report weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent in most human studies, with the loss coming from fat and some lean mass.[1] The American Heart Association and the US National Institute on Aging have described the evidence for broader health benefits as limited or inconclusive.[1] No trial has studied OMAD or 36-hour fasts for facial appearance.

paras: OMAD is classed as a subtype of time-restricted eating, alongside 8 to 12 hour windows, alternate-day fasting and the 5:2 diet.[1] Wikipedia defines it as eating all daily macronutrients within a single window of one to two hours.[1] Fasts longer than 24 hours with only water are called periodic or extended fasts, usually ranging from several days to a few weeks in the literature.[1][7] A 36-hour fast typically means skipping a full day of meals, so that one dinner is followed by the next day's meals being skipped and food resuming at the following breakfast.

The two practices are often combined in looksmaxxing talk: some users run OMAD daily and add an occasional longer fast, while others compare OMAD to water fasting as alternatives for getting lean before a bulk.[2]

Wikipedia describes several intermittent fasting schedules: time-restricted eating within an 8 to 12 hour window, one-meal-a-day fasting, alternate-day fasting (a fast day with under 25 percent of usual energy, alternating with a normal day), and the 5:2 diet of two low-calorie days (about 500 to 600 calories) per week.[1]

The same article describes the fed state lasting about 4 hours with glucose as the main fuel, a postabsorptive state up to about 18 hours using liver glycogen, and a fasted state beginning after roughly 12 to 36 hours when liver glucose is depleted and fat is mobilised and converted into ketones, which some authors call the metabolic switch.[1] A 36-hour fast therefore extends into that fasted state, while a typical OMAD day, with about 22 hours between meals, sits at the edge of it.

Wikipedia's Fasting article adds that early in a longer fast the body relies on making new glucose, a phase linked to roughly two-thirds of early weight loss being lean tissue rather than fat, after which the fat-to-lean ratio of loss is about 7:6 and ketones replace glucose as the main fuel for the nervous system.[7] Circadian research cited on the intermittent fasting page links eating late at night, when melatonin is secreted, with higher glucose levels in young adults.[1]

Fasting is an ancient practice found in Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Jainism and Judaism.[1] In the early 20th century, writers such as Upton Sinclair promoted fasting cures, and in 1932 the physician Morris Fishbein listed fasting among fad diets and warned that prolonged fasting was unnecessary and harmful.[7] Therapeutic intermittent fasts for obesity have been investigated since at least 1915, and medical interest renewed in the 1960s after Bloom and colleagues published an enthusiastic report, with fasts of one to 14 days studied.[1] Wikipedia records the longest documented medically evaluated fast as the 382-day fast of Angus Barbieri in 1965 to 1966.[7]

The 5:2 diet was first documented in a 2011 article co-authored by Michelle Harvie, Mark Mattson and colleagues, and Michael Mosley popularised it in the UK and Australia after a 2012 BBC Horizon documentary, Eat, Fast and Live Longer; his book The Fast Diet, written with Mimi Spencer, followed in early 2013.[1][8] Mosley died in June 2024 while on holiday in Greece.[8]

Wikipedia says intermittent fasting became a trend in Silicon Valley and was named the most popular diet of 2018 by the International Food Information Council.[1] Canadian nephrologist Jason Fung, author of The Complete Guide to Fasting (2016, with Jimmy Moore) and The Obesity Code (2016), has promoted intermittent and extended fasts, usually alongside low-carbohydrate eating.[9] Critics cited on his Wikipedia page, including a Clinical Diabetes author and book reviewers, dispute some of his broader claims about insulin and obesity.[9]

Forum users report using OMAD alongside low-carbohydrate eating or weight-loss medication to reduce fat before a muscle-building phase, and ask whether to choose OMAD or longer water fasts.[2] In one thread a user already on weight-loss medication and aiming to be as lean as possible before starting testosterone and a lean bulk asks whether to water fast or do OMAD low-carb; a reply suggests no-carb, high-fat, high-protein OMAD and cutting fructose.[2]

Other users ask whether OMAD causes hair loss at a daily intake of about 1,500 calories, with one reply saying extreme deficits can cause shedding but that this intake probably would not.[10] Threads also discuss OMAD for morning bloating and growth hormone, with replies varying.[3][11] A user posting about OMAD describes it as feeling like a cheat code for weight loss.[12]

On T Nation, lifters describe OMAD as a practical routine. One training log says low meal frequency fits the author's approach alongside a three-day-a-week program,[4] another lifter chronicles a plan to reach about 10 percent body fat,[5] and others mention settling into OMAD because of life circumstances or using it on non-lifting days to lose leftover fat from a bulk.[13][6] Another poster describes OMAD with protein shakes through the day and notes feeling tired after the large meal.[14]

Practitioners describe OMAD in general terms as one large meal, often in the evening, with water, coffee or tea during the fast. Variants include a keto or low-carbohydrate OMAD, OMAD with protein shakes at other times, and OMAD only on rest days.[2][6][14] The 36-hour fast is usually described as a periodic add-on, used a few times a month by some practitioners, or as a reset between phases of a diet. Athletes and lifters often pair these with resistance training, aiming to preserve muscle while losing fat.[4][5]

Weight loss from intermittent fasting includes fat and some lean mass; for time-restricted eating the fat-to-lean ratio is about 4:1.[1] Umbrella reviews in 2021 and 2024 reported improved weight and cardiometabolic outcomes in overweight or obese adults, with a smaller blood-pressure effect than continuous calorie restriction; the 2024 review listed reductions in waist circumference, fat mass, LDL cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting insulin.[1] A 2021 Cochrane review found it unclear whether intermittent fasting prevents cardiovascular disease.[1] A 2026 review in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition discussed impacts, mechanisms and cautions of intermittent fasting.[15]

The American Heart Association said there was no good evidence of heart-health benefit, and the US National Institute on Aging, in 2018, did not recommend such diets for the general public.[1] A 2019 NEJM review by Rafael de Cabo and Mark Mattson described the evidence as preliminary and long-term effects as unstudied.[1] A 2017 randomized trial of alternate-day fasting in metabolically healthy obese adults examined weight loss, maintenance and cardioprotection.[1]

A 2025 review found no consistent effect of 12-hour fasting on attention, working memory or other cognitive tasks.[1] On exercise, Wikipedia reports that athletic performance does not benefit from intermittent fasting and that overnight fasting before exercise increases fat breakdown but reduces performance in prolonged exercise over 60 minutes.[1] Lifters on T Nation describe training on OMAD and reporting good results, which are individual accounts rather than trials.[4][5]

A 2025 case report described a 42-year-old man with class III obesity and prediabetes managed with a supervised one-meal-a-day pattern.[16] Forum users who report 'cheat code' weight loss are describing individual experience, not a controlled study.[12]

Reported effects include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, which one review says fade within about a month; a 2018 systematic review reported no major adverse effects.[1] Dropout rates in a 2019 review ranged from 2 to 38 percent for intermittent fasting versus 0 to 50 percent for calorie restriction.[1] Reduced gallbladder movement and cholesterol-rich bile during rapid fat loss are reported to raise gallstone risk.[7] Longer fasts can lower sodium, potassium and magnesium, and refeeding syndrome is described after about four to five days without food.[7]

Intermittent fasting is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, growing children and adolescents, older adults, people who are not overweight, or people with or vulnerable to eating disorders; it has not been studied in children, older adults or underweight people.[1] The UK's NHS advises people considering the 5:2 diet to consult a physician first, New Zealand's Ministry of Health says it can cause hunger, low energy and poor mental functioning, and the American Diabetes Association found limited evidence for type 1 diabetes.[1]

Trials have examined time-restricted eating and alternate-day fasting rather than OMAD or 36-hour fasts specifically. A 2018 pilot study of 23 obese adults eating within an 8-hour window reported reduced body weight. The 2011 Harvie trial in young overweight women compared intermittent with continuous energy restriction, and a 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine trial tested alternate-day fasting in obese adults.[1] No studies found on OMAD or 36-hour fasts for facial appearance.

OMAD is discussed on looksmax.org alongside water fasting, low-carbohydrate eating and weight-loss medication, as a tool for fat loss before building muscle.[2] Threads ask whether it prevents morning bloating, whether it raises growth hormone, and whether it affects hair.[10][3][11] Wikipedia notes that intermittent fasting is described as a fad diet with celebrity endorsements and that, by 2019, companies selling coaching, supplements and meal packages had been criticised for expensive products not backed by science.[1]

lore.intro: Forum threads discuss OMAD as a way to cut fat and manage hunger, often combined with low-carbohydrate eating.[2][10]
